counterexample: The inference 'f(z) = O(z^{-1}) implies f'(z) = O(z^{-1})' is false in general: f(x) = sin(x^3)/x satisfies |f(x)| <= 1/x for x > 1, yet f'(x) = 3x cos(x^3) - sin(x^3)/x^2 is unbounded, so it is not O(x^{-1}). Hence the bound quoted in line 0011 on the error term R(z) = ln Gamma(z) - ((z - 1/2) ln z - z + (ln 2*pi)/2) does not 'directly' yield any bound on R'(z), which is the third term of (1). (In the actual setting the conclusion is true, but only via analyticity of R plus a Cauchy estimate on a disc of radius proportional to |z| inside the sector |arg z| < pi - epsilon, giving R'(z) = O(z^{-2}); the proof never invokes analyticity or any such argument.) Additionally, the bound as literally written in 0011, c/|z^{-1}| = c|z|, is the reciprocal of the intended c|z|^{-1} and is far too weak to support even a correct differentiation argument.
reasoning_summary: Steps 0001-0003 correctly quote the Stirling/log-Gamma asymptotic ln Gamma(z) = (z - 1/2) ln z - z + (ln 2*pi)/2 + O(z^{-1}). Step 0005-0007 is acceptable if the O-term is read as the concrete analytic remainder R(z) defined as the difference of the two sides: differentiating the explicit part gives ln z + (z - 1/2)/z - 1 = ln z - 1/(2z), and Gamma'(z)/Gamma(z) is the derivative of ln Gamma(z), so (1) holds with third term R'(z). Step 0009-0011 states a size bound on R itself; as written the right-hand side is c/|z^{-1}| = c|z| rather than the intended c/|z|, and the left-hand inequality (-c|z| < |R|) is vacuous, but the assertion is at least not false. Step 0013 is where the proof fails: it concludes 'directly' that the third term of (1), namely R'(z), is O(z^{-1}) from a magnitude bound on R. A bound on a function gives no bound on its derivative without further input (here: analyticity of R on the sector plus a Cauchy estimate). The step is a non sequitur, and it is the only substantive step supporting the theorem's error term, so the proof as given is invalid despite the statement being true.
